chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'a, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Murazm, from 'Ammar al-Sabati, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The deceased has the strongest claim to his wealth as long as the soul is present and he can speak with it; if he says 'after me,' it is not for him except for one-third. The other view in the report containing the bequest of more than one-third is that we interpret it as: if it was in the presence of the heirs and they approved it, then that is permissible, which indicates that.

key_terms.الرُّوحُ: The soul (indicating the state of near-death)
key_terms.يَبِينُ بِهِ: He speaks with it (referring to the dying breath)

ai.seo_question: What is the limit of a bequest in Shia jurisprudence and can heirs approve more than one-third?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Istibsar clarifies the transition of ownership from the dying person to the heirs, emphasizing that the 'right' to dispose of wealth ceases at death, limiting the bequest to one-third. It introduces a crucial juristic nuance: if the bequest exceeds one-third, it is valid provided the heirs consent while the person is still alive and speaking, effectively treating it as a gift inter vivos rather than a posthumous will. This reflects the Shia scholarly approach to reconciling textual limits with practical family agreements.
